client: Lately, I've been feeling completely drained trying to keep up with everything. No matter how many hours I put into studying or working my part-time job, I'm constantly worried my grades will slip. I know therapy is supposed to help, but I'm not sure how talking about it will actually give me more hours in the day.
therapist: I hear how overwhelmed you're feeling, trying to balance everything while still worrying it's not enough. It might help to explore whether these thoughts about needing to do more are based on facts or fears - would you be open to looking at that together?

client: I guess they're mostly fears... but they feel so real in the moment. Like last night I stayed up until 3am rewriting a paper that was already decent, because I kept imagining my professor thinking "this student isn't cut out for this program." Even though rationally I know that's probably not true.
therapist: It sounds like that automatic thought about your professor's opinion had such a powerful grip on you that it overrode your rational awareness of the paper's quality. What do you think might happen if you experimented with submitting work at your earlier "decent" stage sometimes?

client: I don't know... the idea of submitting something before it's "perfect" makes me really anxious. What if I get a lower grade because I didn't put in those extra hours? Then I'll prove to myself that I wasn't good enough after all. It feels like I'm setting myself up to fail.
therapist: That fear of proving yourself "not good enough" carries so much weight, doesn't it? Let's gently examine whether those extra hours actually lead to significantly better grades, or if they might be more about soothing the anxiety itself. How do you typically feel after pulling those all-nighters to perfect your work?

client: Honestly? Exhausted and kind of numb. The weird thing is my grades on those "perfect" papers aren't actually much better than when I turn things in earlier. But I still can't shake the feeling that if I don't do this, I'll regret it. It's like I'm addicted to the reassurance even though I know it doesn't really pay off.
therapist: It's so insightful that you recognize this pattern - the temporary reassurance comes at a high cost of exhaustion, yet the pull remains strong. What do you imagine might happen if you treated this like breaking any other habit, starting with small steps while noticing the uncomfortable feelings that arise?

client: I could maybe try turning in one small assignment without rewriting it to death... but even thinking about that makes my chest feel tight. What if I pick the wrong assignment to experiment with and it backfires spectacularly? Part of me feels like this perfectionism is the only thing keeping me from totally failing.
therapist: That chest tightness shows how deeply this pattern is tied to your sense of safety and success. Let's work together to choose an assignment where the stakes feel manageable, while we explore how perfectionism might actually be holding you back rather than protecting you from failure. How does that approach feel to you?

client: I guess it feels... scary but maybe worth trying. There's a weekly reading response due Friday that's only worth 5% of our grade. But I'm worried that even if I try this small step, I'll just end up obsessing over all the other assignments instead. The anxiety has to go somewhere, right?
therapist: It's understandable that the anxiety feels like it needs an outlet - that shows how hard your mind has been working to protect you. This could be a chance to observe what happens to that anxiety when you don't feed it with perfectionism, like watching a wave that eventually recedes. Would you be willing to note what the anxiety does throughout that day after submitting the reading response?

client: I could try writing down how anxious I feel before and after submitting it... but part of me is already bracing for disaster. What if that one assignment is the difference between an A and a B later? It feels irresponsible not to obsess about every single point.
therapist: I hear how powerful that "what if" feels—like you're gambling with your future by not chasing every point. Let's gently challenge that by asking: When you look back at previous semesters, can you recall a single small assignment that actually made that much difference in the end?

client: Thinking back, I can't actually remember any small assignments that made a huge difference... but it still feels risky to stop trying so hard. What if this is the semester where it does matter? I think part of me believes that if I just work hard enough, I can guarantee good outcomes, even though I know that's not really true.
therapist: That belief that extreme effort can guarantee safety is so understandable—it's given you a sense of control during stressful times. What do you think it would mean about you if you discovered that good outcomes can happen without exhausting yourself in this way?

client: That's actually really uncomfortable to think about... because then I'd have to face that all this suffering wasn't necessary after all. And if I'm not pushing myself to the limit, who even am I? Being the "hard worker" has become such a big part of my identity.
therapist: It sounds like this realization touches on something deeply personal - how much of your self-worth has become tied to this identity as someone who constantly pushes themselves. What might it feel like to explore who you are beyond being the "hard worker," and what other parts of yourself you might want to nurture?

client: That idea makes me feel uneasy because I don't really know who I am without the constant striving. I've always defined myself by my achievements and how much I can push through. The thought of letting go of that feels like I'd be losing my sense of purpose or direction.
therapist: It's understandable that this feels so unsettling—your accomplishments and perseverance have been such important anchors for your sense of self. This could be an opportunity to gently explore what truly matters to you beyond external achievements. What values or interests might you want to nurture if you weren't so focused on constantly proving yourself?
